report:
**Conclusion:** Yes. Denosumab (Prolia) reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in osteoporosis—most clearly demonstrated in postmenopausal women at high fracture risk. In the 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial, new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 2.3% of women receiving denosumab versus 7.2% receiving placebo, a **68% relative risk reduction**. It also reduced hip and nonvertebral fractures.

This benefit is reflected in the U.S. prescribing information, which states that Prolia reduces vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fracture incidence in postmenopausal osteoporosis. A major clinical guide likewise estimates vertebral-fracture reduction at about 68% within one year.

An important caveat: denosumab must be administered consistently (60 mg subcutaneously every six months) and should not be stopped or substantially delayed without a clinician-directed transition to another antiresorptive medicine, because rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures can occur after discontinuation. Appropriateness depends on fracture risk, kidney function/hypocalcemia risk, dental considerations, and alternative treatments.
